complexity.notes: Dropping the previous version's sort loses nothing: the nums[i:] slicing already enforces a canonical order over combinations, so sorting was never load-bearing. Each call slices nums[i:] and builds [nums[i]] + x, adding O(n) and O(depth) copying per tree node; these are absorbed in the reported tree-size bound, though carrying a single path list with append/pop would avoid them. The `target in nums` check is a linear scan per call, likewise absorbed. Space quoted is for the recursion stack, where each frame retains its own slice; the output list itself can be exponentially large in t.
complexity.summary: Pure top-down recursion: for each index i, prepend nums[i] to every combination of nums[i:] summing to target - nums[i], plus a direct [target] hit when target appears in nums; recursing only over the suffix nums[i:] prevents duplicate combinations. In the bounds, n = len(nums), t = target, m = min(nums): the recursion tree has depth at most t/m and branching n, so its size is O(n^(t/m)), equivalently O(k * t/m) output-sensitive for k output combinations.
